questions.title: How are continuous feature thresholds chosen when LLMs generate rules in FeatLLM?
questions.question_body: In FeatLLM, the LLM produces human-readable rules that often look like inequalities (e.g., "age > 60"). With only few-shot examples, how does the LLM decide specific threshold values for continuous features? Are these thresholds inferred purely from prior knowledge, from the provided few-shot examples, or both? If both, what prevents overfitting to arbitrary cut points suggested by tiny k-shot samples? Do you post-process or discretize continuous features before prompting to stabilize the learned thresholds?

questions.title: Why constrain rule weights to be non-negative in the linear model?
questions.question_body: Section 3.2 defines logits per class as \(\text{logit}_k^i = \max(\mathbf{w}_k, 0) \cdot \mathbf{z}_k^i\), forcing non-negative contributions from rule activations. Conceptually, this prevents a rule that fires from ever decreasing a class's logit. But some rules might indicate negative evidence for a class (e.g., "no chest pain" might reduce the likelihood of heart disease). Why prohibit negative weights? Is the intent that negative evidence is represented as positive evidence for some other class, making explicit negatives unnecessary? Did you empirically compare against an unconstrained linear/logistic model with signed weights?

questions.title: How are contradictory or overlapping rules handled during training and inference?
questions.question_body: FeatLLM extracts a fixed number (e.g., 10) of rules per class. What happens if two rules for the same class are logically overlapping or contradictory (e.g., "age > 65" and "age > 70", or "smoker == yes" vs. a composite rule that implies "smoker == no")? During training, will both rules just receive weights based on usefulness, or is there any deduplication/logic simplification step? Does the LLM get guidance to avoid redundant rules, and how do you ensure stability when overlapping rules correlate strongly, potentially causing multicollinearity in the binary feature space?

questions.title: How is multi-class classification formulated with per-class rule sets and softmax?
questions.question_body: For multi-class tasks, you build R binary rule features per class and then compute per-class logits before applying softmax. Suppose a sample satisfies many rules for multiple classes. Does the softmax inherently resolve competition, or do you normalize rule counts/weights across classes to handle class-specific differences in the number or "generality" of rules? Also, what happens when a sample satisfies none of the rules for any class—do all logits become zero, leading to a uniform softmax output?

questions.title: What specific bagging scheme is used for samples and features in FeatLLM?
questions.question_body: The paper says you use feature bagging and instance bagging to control prompt size and induce diversity, but the exact sampling scheme is not specified. Do you sample without replacement from features and examples for each LLM call? What are the typical fractions for features and examples retained per trial, and how are they tuned? Are the same subsets used for both the rule-generation prompt and the subsequent weight training, or is there a risk of distribution shift between the prompt subset and the training subset?

questions.title: How are categorical features and multi-valued categories represented in rules and parsing?
questions.question_body: For categorical columns with many levels (e.g., dozens or hundreds), how does the LLM express rules—single-category equality, sets of categories, or regex-like patterns? Does the response template explicitly allow OR-clauses over categories, and can the parser robustly translate natural language descriptions of sets into code (e.g., {"A", "B", "C"})? How do you handle high-cardinality categories where enumerations inflate prompt length or lead to brittle parsing?

questions.title: How robust is the rule-to-code parsing when LLMs vary syntax (e.g., "<" vs. "less than")?
questions.question_body: You mention leveraging the LLM itself to generate Python code from natural-language rules to mitigate noisy syntax. What safeguards exist if the generated code is syntactically valid but semantically incorrect (e.g., off-by-one thresholds, inclusive vs. exclusive bounds)? Do you run any unit checks on toy inputs to validate rule behavior against the natural-language description? Also, how do you handle missing values in code generation (e.g., null-safe comparisons) to avoid runtime errors?

questions.title: Security implications of using exec() for generated code in FeatLLM?
questions.question_body: The method executes LLM-generated code via Python's exec(). What sandboxing measures are in place to prevent file system or network access, arbitrary imports, or long-running loops? Do you restrict the available builtins/modules or run the code in a containerized environment? Given industrial deployment is a stated goal, can you detail the threat model and mitigations you applied when executing model-generated code?

questions.title: How is k-fold cross-validation used with very small k-shot training sets?
questions.question_body: You select epochs using k-fold cross-validation to avoid overfitting in the linear model trained on rule features. In very low-shot scenarios (e.g., 4 or 8 shots), how do you define folds without collapsing class coverage? The paper says k is 2 or 4, ensuring each fold has at least one example per class. Does this procedure become unstable for multi-class datasets with class imbalance? Did you compare against leave-one-out or stratified repeated holdouts to reduce variance in model selection?

questions.title: How are few-shot examples chosen for the prompt, and does example order bias results?
questions.question_body: You mention randomizing the order of few-shot demonstrations because order affects LLM responses. How are the specific examples selected from the k-shot pool—randomly, or with some coverage heuristic (e.g., class balance, feature diversity)? Given that different orders and selections induce different rules, did you evaluate strategies for selecting exemplars that reduce variance or improve performance (e.g., clustering-based prototypes or informative selection), versus pure random choice?

questions.title: What prevents label leakage through feature names or descriptions?
questions.question_body: Because FeatLLM includes detailed feature names and descriptions in the prompt, and some tabular datasets contain columns that are proxies for the label (or include subtle task hints), how do you ensure there is no leakage (e.g., a feature named "disease_present")? Do you sanitize feature names/descriptions or mask obviously label-correlated strings? In the synthetic datasets, was any care taken to avoid textual cues that trivially reveal the target?

questions.title: Why fix the number of rules per class (e.g., 10), and how sensitive is performance?
questions.question_body: The paper fixes the number of rules per class to 10 and shows minimal sensitivity, yet acknowledges trade-offs with prompt length and overfitting. Conceptually, some tasks may need fewer, more general rules, while others may benefit from many specialized rules. Did you try adaptive stopping criteria (e.g., based on validation improvement or rule novelty)? Also, do you allow nested logic or only flat conjunctions/disjunctions per rule, and how does expressivity trade off against interpretability and stability?

questions.title: How does FeatLLM handle samples that match zero rules or all rules?
questions.question_body: Since features are binary per rule, edge cases can occur. If a sample activates zero rules for all classes, logits become zero and softmax is uniform—do you treat this as an abstention or low-confidence prediction? Conversely, if the sample activates almost all rules for multiple classes, do you cap contributions or regularize weights to avoid overconfident predictions? Is there any calibration step applied after ensembling to improve probability quality?

questions.title: Details on ensembling: averaging probabilities vs. logits and calibration effects
questions.question_body: The paper states that final predictions average class probabilities \(\mathbf{p}^i\) across T trials. Did you compare against averaging logits or stacking (e.g., training a meta-learner on the ensemble outputs)? Averaging probabilities can under- or over-calibrate depending on diversity. Did you measure calibration metrics (e.g., ECE, Brier score) and try temperature scaling or Dirichlet calibration on top of the ensemble?

questions.title: How fair is the comparison to TabLLM when using T0 instead of GPT-3.5?
questions.question_body: In experiments, FeatLLM uses GPT-3.5 for rule generation, while TabLLM is restricted to public checkpoints (T0). Since base model capability can significantly affect downstream performance, how do you ensure a fair comparison? Did you attempt a variant where FeatLLM uses the same open-source LLM as TabLLM, or a variant where TabLLM uses the strongest permissible model? Can you quantify the expected performance delta attributable to backbone differences rather than method design?

questions.title: What is the exact objective and regularization used for weight tuning on binary rule features?
questions.question_body: The linear model is trained with cross-entropy over softmaxed per-class logits. Are there any regularizers (e.g., L1 to encourage sparsity over rules, L2 for stability) applied to \(\mathbf{w}_k\)? Given potentially noisy or redundant rules, did you study the effect of L1 on pruning spurious rules vs. relying solely on weight magnitudes? Also, why 200 epochs with Adam and LR 0.01—did you perform sensitivity analysis to avoid overfitting in the tiny-sample regime?

questions.title: How do you measure and filter "useful" rules before and after tuning?
questions.question_body: The paper reports the fraction of rules with AUROC > 0.5 against the target ("Before tuning") and then filters rules with learned weights below 0.1 ("After tuning"). Why AUROC > 0.5 as the usefulness threshold and 0.1 for weights—are these data-dependent? Also, AUROC on very low-shot data can be high-variance; did you use any cross-validated or bootstrapped estimate to assess rule usefulness robustly before final filtering?
